extracted.intended_audience: writers and students of fiction (novelists, literature students, literary critics)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for creating and handling characters, their relation to plot and other novel elements, and how novels treat core human experiences (birth, food, sleep, love, death). Emphasises devices such as point of view and the distinction between flat and round characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novel versus memoir/history (character identity)
rubrics_metrics.description: “If a character in a novel is exactly like Queen Victoria—not rather like but exactly like—then it actually is Queen Victoria, and the novel, or all of it that the character touches, becomes a memoir. A memoir is history, it is based on evidence. A novel is based on evidence + or — x, the unknown quantity being the temperament of the novelist, and the unknown quantity always modifies the effect of the evidence, and sometimes transforms it entirely.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reproduce real persons exactly if you intend fiction; the novelist must add or subtract (the novelist’s temperament) to transform evidence into fiction. Maintaining a distinguishable fictional identity (not exact historical replication) keeps a work a novel rather than memoir.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function of the novelist — reveal the hidden/inner life
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is the function of the novelist to reveal the hidden life at its source: to tell us more about Queen Victoria than could be known, and thus to produce a character who is not the Queen Victoria of history.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelists should aim to expose inner motives, dreams and private thoughts beyond the external evidence available to historians; inventiveness in inner life is a proper and central novelist’s task.

rubrics_metrics.name: History vs novel: actions vs inner causation / intentionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Paraphrase of Alain: the fictitious element is not so much the story as the method by which thought develops into action; history emphasises external causes and fatality, whereas the novel is founded on human nature and intentionality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When representing behaviour, the novelist privileges internal psychological causation and intention over deterministic external explanation. The method of showing thought turning into action (even if unlike daily life) is a legitimate and defining device of fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definiteness of fictional characters (completeness of knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: “People in a novel can be understood completely by the reader, if the novelist wishes; their inner as well as their outer life can be exposed… we have been told all about them that can be told; even if they are imperfect or unreal they do not contain any secrets.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A character’s reality in fiction relies on the novelist supplying enough inner and outer detail that the reader gets a sense of full (or explicable) knowledge; completeness or the impression of explicability makes characters convincing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five basic human experiences as novelistic material: birth, food, sleep, love, death
rubrics_metrics.description: “The main facts in human life are five: birth, food, sleep, love and death.” The author asks how novelists reproduce, exaggerate, minimize or ignore these facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these five experiences as axes for characterization and plotting, but be conscious of common novelistic tendencies (see separate entries for each). Decide whether to reproduce them realistically or adapt them for artistic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of birth in fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Birth is an experience we only know by report and cannot remember; novelists usually 'pick up' characters after birth and few novelists attempt to reconstruct baby psychology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you choose to portray birth or infancy, be aware it is rarely represented and can be a source of novel material — but many authors avoid it for practical/narrative reasons. Decide whether to exploit that neglected area or follow convention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of death in fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Death is ‘nourished much more on observation’ and is congenial to novelists because it ends a book neatly; the novelist can follow characters through death imaginatively but should avoid bringing in séance-like scraps about 'life beyond.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use death both as a dramatic closure and as an opportunity for rich, observed detail; keep any transcendental material imaginative and consistent with the novel’s tone rather than sentimental or spurious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of food in fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Food in fiction is mainly social: it draws characters together, but they seldom require it physiologically, seldom enjoy it, and novels often miss its sensuous/aesthetic side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether food will serve as social/cultural signalling or be rendered sensuously to enrich atmosphere; be conscious that many novels underuse the immediate, sensuous aspects of eating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of sleep and dreams in fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Sleep is usually perfunctory; dreams are introduced with a purpose and not used to represent the character’s overall life; novelists rarely recreate the full dream-world or the fact that a third of life is spent asleep.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you employ dreams or sleep-scenes, do so deliberately — they should serve a specific narrative purpose or reveal a facet of character, rather than acting as filler or an ungrounded symbol. Consider whether to attempt a fuller rendering of sleep or remain selective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of love/sexual/emotional life in fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Love is hugely prominent in novels and often overemphasised; characters tend to be unduly sensitive to love, partly reflecting the novelist’s own state and partly because love conveniently ends books (marriage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid making love the default centre of every plot unless you consciously intend that emphasis. Be wary of monotony; consider other motives and emotions, and resist using love merely as a convenient closure (e.g., marriage-as-resolution) without nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial omniscience as criterion of character 'reality'
rubrics_metrics.description: “A character in a book is real: it is real when the novelist knows everything about it. He may not choose to tell us all he knows… but he will give us the feeling that though the character has not been explained, it is explicable.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The writer’s deep, implicit knowledge of a character (even if not fully disclosed) is what convinces readers; cultivate full backstory and motivations so you can selectively reveal details that create the impression of plenary understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters must adapt to plot and other fictional requirements (coherence/integration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters arrive with their own impulses and may 'get out of hand' or be treasonous to the book’s scheme; they must adapt to story, moral, fellow characters, atmosphere, etc., or else the book may break or decay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance character autonomy with structural needs: allow believable independence but ensure characters function coherently within plot, theme, and the novel’s overall design. Too much freedom can fragment the work; too much control can deaden it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flat characters (definition and use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Flat characters (called 'humorous' in the 17th century) are constructed around a single idea or quality and can be expressed in one sentence (e.g., 'I never will desert Mr. Micawber'). They provide convenience and remain unchanging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use flat characters when you need immediate recognition, comic or thematic clarity, durability in the reader’s memory, or elements that don’t require development. They are useful counters and fixtures in a narrative fabric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Round characters (definition and function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Round characters have multiple factors and facets, change through scenes, are complex and cannot be summed up in a single phrase (e.g., Becky Sharp). They are remembered through their development and scenes rather than a single formula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose round characters when psychological complexity, development, and dramatic transformation are central to your aims. Expect them to require more narrative space and to interact intricately with plot and other characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdependence of characters in complex novels (parallel, not coincide, with life)
rubrics_metrics.description: In novels like Jane Austen’s the characters are inter-dependent and bound by many ties; a character as a whole parallels life rather than coinciding with it, and cannot be transplanted without the surrounding context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a densely woven novel, design characters’ relations, social ties and setting as mutually constraining; realism of a character often depends on its network of connections rather than isolated presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing mundane needs in fiction (homo fictus vs homo sapiens)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fictional beings (homo fictus) often are born 'off', need little food or sleep, and are tireless in human relationships; they differ from real people because the narrator and creator are one and can expose secret lives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide how much to minimize or include ordinary needs (food, sleep, routines) in service of narrative pacing and thematic focus. Minimizing mundane needs can heighten concentration on relationships and ideas, but over-minimization risks implausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view as a device for solving novelistic difficulties
rubrics_metrics.description: The author names point of view as a principal device (alongside use of different character kinds) for handling the novelist’s problems of control and exposure of inner life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a point of view that controls how much of a character’s hidden life is visible, that harmonises with the desired level of omniscience or opacity, and that helps manage character freedom versus narrative coherence.
